idiom_name: logging chokepoint + chained MAC + anchored off-host verifier
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: route every security-relevant record through one logging chokepoint; serialise it deterministically; compute mac_i = MAC(key, mac_{i-1} || seq_i || canonical_record_i); append record, sequence number and authenticator to a store the application can only append to; publish the head authenticator out of band; and verify the whole chain with a separate tool that holds the verification key and the anchor. Keep keys, the anchor and verification outside the recording trust boundary, define per event class whether a logging failure fails the operation, and treat every logged field as untrusted data (log injection, secrets, personal data).
code_sketch:
logger.audit(event):
    rec = canonicalise(event)                 # stable field order, UTC, redacted
    seq, prev = state.next()
    mac = hmac(key, prev || seq || rec)       # chained authenticator, not a per-record hash
    store.append(seq, rec, mac)               # append-only, durability per policy
    state.commit(seq, mac)
# verifier (off host): mac_i == hmac(key, mac_{i-1} || seq_i || rec_i) and head == anchor
pitfalls: Chaining only the record body, leaving sequence number and timestamp outside the authenticated bytes - records can then be reordered or replayed while every digest still verifies.
Verifying inside the trust boundary that writes (same host, same key), so the attacker the pattern is meant to detect simply recomputes the chain.
Forgetting the anchor: truncation of the newest records is invisible until the head authenticator is published somewhere the writer cannot reach.

Wrong move: accepting a record whose authenticator is valid under any live key, with key id and epoch outside the authenticated bytes -> a compromised writer re-seals tampered old records with the current key, exactly the CVE-2023-31439 class broken in journald's sealing until systemd 255 -> bind the key id (and epoch) into the MAC input and have the verifier check each record's key epoch against its sequence position.

Wrong move: committing the in-memory prev/sequence state before the append is durable, or assuming it survives a crash -> a crash between state update and fsync forks the chain or reuses a (prev, seq) pair, so the verifier sees a false tamper - or a silent duplicate - at the worst possible moment -> append and fsync first, update chain state only after the write succeeded, and rebuild head state from the durable tail on restart.

Wrong move: verifying only the current head authenticator or the record count -> a rewrite that re-chains from a chosen point plus a rollback to an older head passes a spot check -> replay contiguously from the last externally anchored sequence number and treat any head regression as tampering.
